column1: # The parser has test-data/protocol-fixtures.tsv, read by all three implementations. The
# validator had nothing equivalent: its Python and JavaScript versions were hand-ports held
# together by two sets of similarly-named tests, which is agreement by convention rather
# than by construction. This file is the construction.
# A validator that disagrees with the other one miscounts packet loss, duplicates or
# reboots — the numbers an operator judges a live link by, and the ones a post-flight
# Format: <scenario> TAB <expected team, or '-'> TAB <expect> TAB <packet>
# Rows of one scenario are consecutive and are fed to a fresh validator in file order.
# <expect> is a comma-separated set describing the report for that packet:
#   missing=N  N packets never arrived before this one
#   restart    recognised as a vehicle reboot
#   wrongteam  rejected: not the expected team
#   tsreg      the mission clock went backwards
#   gpsrej     the GPS fix is implausible; the packet is still kept
# Blank lines and lines starting with '#' are ignored. Whitespace inside the packet is
# significant; do not reformat this file.
# A clean stream is the baseline: nothing flagged, nothing counted.
# A gap counts the packets that never arrived, not the fact that there was a gap.
# A repeat of a number already seen is a duplicate, and does not advance the sequence.
# A late packet that fills nothing: P-003 already counted P-002 as missing.
# The watchdog is designed to reboot the vehicle. Counter back to P-001 AND the mission
# clock back to zero: that is a restart, not a flood of duplicates for the rest of the
# flight. The clock going backwards is not separately reported as a regression here: a
# recognised restart clears the reference it would have been compared against, which is the
# difference between "the vehicle rebooted" and "the vehicle's clock misbehaved".
# A P-001 without a clock regression is a corrupted packet number, not a reboot. Both
# signals are required, and this is the case that proves the second one is load-bearing.
# The first packet of a session can never be a restart: there is nothing to restart from.
# Another team's packet is rejected outright and never reaches the sequence logic.
# A clock that goes backwards without a counter restart is noted, and the packet is kept.
# An impossible fix is flagged, and the packet is still kept: the mandatory fields in it
# are as good as any other packet's.
# With no expected team configured, any well-formed team id is accepted.
# GPS altitude. Latitude and longitude have mathematical bounds and were always checked;
# altitude has none, so nothing checked it -- in any of the three implementations. A
# corrupted altitude field reads as a place, and lands on the barometric-against-GPS
# correlation graph the runbook scores. The bounds are loose on purpose: -1000 m to
# 80000 m catches corruption without second-guessing the receiver.
# A fix is a latitude and a longitude. An absent altitude is not an implausible fix.
